cards.front: Which AWS service runs serverless SQL queries directly on files stored in Amazon S3?
cards.back: **Amazon Athena**. No cluster to manage; tables are metadata in the Glue Data Catalog and you pay per data scanned.

cards.front: How is Athena SQL on S3 priced by default, and what does that imply?
cards.back: About **USD 5 per TB scanned** per query. Reducing bytes scanned (columnar formats, compression, partitions) cuts both cost and run time. Capacity Reservations (per DPU-hour) are an alternative for steady heavy use.
cards.updated: Capacity Reservations are a newer pricing option not on the slides

cards.front: Name four ways to make Athena queries cheaper and faster.
cards.back: 1. Store data in a **columnar** format (**Parquet** or **ORC**). 2. **Compress** it. 3. **Partition** it by commonly filtered columns (`year=2026/month=10/`). 4. Use **fewer, larger files** (around 128 MB or more) instead of many tiny ones.

cards.front: What is Athena Federated Query?
cards.back: Running one SQL query across non-S3 sources (RDS, Aurora, DynamoDB, Redshift, CloudWatch Logs, on-premises JDBC databases...) through **data source connectors**, traditionally Lambda functions. Results are stored in S3.

cards.front: Which open-source engine does Athena engine version 3 track?
cards.back: **Trino** (alongside Presto). The slides say Presto; engine v3 integrates improvements from both projects, and its function reference points to Trino.
cards.updated: Slides say Athena is built on Presto; engine version 3 follows Trino and Presto

cards.front: OLTP or OLAP: which one is Amazon Redshift built for?
cards.back: **OLAP** (analytics and data warehousing). It is columnar with a massively parallel query engine. Use RDS, Aurora or DynamoDB for OLTP application traffic.

cards.front: What do the leader node and compute nodes do in a Redshift cluster?
cards.back: The **leader node** receives SQL, plans the query and aggregates the final results. **Compute nodes** execute their part of the plan in parallel and send intermediate results back to the leader.

cards.front: Redshift provisioned vs Redshift Serverless: how do you pay?
cards.back: **Provisioned**: per node-hour for the node type and count you choose (reserved nodes for 1 or 3 years save money). **Serverless**: per **RPU-hour** only while queries run, per-second billing with a 60-second minimum; base capacity from 4 RPUs.
cards.updated: Serverless minimum base capacity is now 4 RPUs

cards.front: How often does Redshift take automated snapshots, and how long are they kept?
cards.back: About every **8 hours** or every **5 GB per node** of changed data, whichever comes first (or on a custom schedule). Retention is **1 to 35 days** (default 1). Manual snapshots are kept until you delete them.

cards.front: How do you set up disaster recovery for Redshift in another Region?
cards.back: Enable **automatic cross-Region snapshot copy**. Automated and manual snapshots are copied to the DR Region, where you restore a **new** cluster if needed.

cards.front: What is the most efficient way to load large amounts of data into Redshift?
cards.back: The **`COPY` command** from S3 (parallel load using an IAM role), or Amazon Data Firehose, which stages to S3 and runs `COPY` for you. Avoid single-row `INSERT`s; if an app must insert, batch the rows.

cards.front: What does Redshift Enhanced VPC Routing do?
cards.back: Forces `COPY` and `UNLOAD` traffic between Redshift and data stores such as S3 through **your VPC**, so VPC endpoints, endpoint policies, security groups, NACLs and Flow Logs apply instead of the internet path.

cards.front: What is Redshift Spectrum, and what does it require?
cards.back: A Redshift feature that queries data **in S3 without loading it**, using external tables and a large fleet of Spectrum nodes. It requires an existing **Redshift cluster** (or Serverless workgroup) to submit the query; RA3 and DC2 clusters must be in the same Region as the bucket.
cards.updated: RG clusters and Redshift Serverless query S3 with their own engine and can reach buckets in other Regions

cards.front: Which Redshift feature replicates Aurora, RDS or DynamoDB data into Redshift without building an ETL pipeline?
cards.back: **Zero-ETL integrations**. After an initial load, changes are replicated continuously into a Redshift provisioned cluster or Serverless namespace.
cards.updated: Zero-ETL integrations are not covered on the slides

cards.front: When would you put Amazon OpenSearch Service next to DynamoDB?
cards.back: When users must **search on any field** or by **partial text match**, which DynamoDB cannot do efficiently (only keys and indexes). DynamoDB stays the source of truth; Streams + Lambda (or the zero-ETL integration) keep the OpenSearch index updated.

cards.front: Two ways to stream CloudWatch Logs into OpenSearch, and their latency?
cards.back: A subscription filter to a **Lambda function** (created by the CloudWatch console) = **real time**; a subscription filter to **Amazon Data Firehose** = **near real time** (buffered).

cards.front: What are the three EMR node types, and which belongs on Spot?
cards.back: **Primary** (coordinates the cluster), **core** (runs tasks and stores HDFS data), **task** (runs tasks only, no HDFS). Put **task nodes on Spot**: an interruption loses compute, not data.
cards.updated: EMR now calls the master node the primary node

cards.front: Besides clusters on EC2, which other ways can you run Amazon EMR?
cards.back: **EMR on EKS** (jobs on an existing Kubernetes cluster) and **EMR Serverless** (Spark or Hive jobs with no cluster to configure or scale).
cards.updated: EMR on EKS and EMR Serverless are not on the slides

cards.front: What is SPICE in Amazon Quick Sight?
cards.back: The **Super-fast, Parallel, In-memory Calculation Engine**. Data imported into SPICE is served from memory, so dashboards are fast and don't query the source (for example Athena) every time.

cards.front: In Quick Sight, how do you limit which columns of a dataset some users can see?
cards.back: **Column-level security (CLS)**, available in **Enterprise** edition. Access is granted to Quick Sight users and groups, which are managed inside the service rather than as IAM users.

cards.front: What must you do before sharing a Quick Sight dashboard, and what can viewers see?
cards.back: You must **publish** the analysis as a dashboard (a read-only copy that keeps filters, parameters, controls and sort order). Viewers of a dashboard can also see the **underlying data**.

cards.front: What is the AWS Glue Data Catalog, and which services use it?
cards.back: A central **metadata** store (databases, tables, schemas, partitions), usually filled by **Glue crawlers**. **Athena**, **Redshift Spectrum**, **EMR** and Glue ETL jobs all read it. It stores no data itself.

cards.front: Which Glue feature prevents an ETL job from reprocessing data it already handled?
cards.back: **Job bookmarks**. They track processed S3 objects or JDBC rows so each run handles only new data.

cards.front: Glue DataBrew vs Glue Studio: what is each for?
cards.back: **DataBrew**: visual data preparation (clean and normalise) with hundreds of prebuilt transformations, for analysts. **Glue Studio**: visual editor to build, run and monitor Glue ETL jobs.

cards.front: What does AWS Lake Formation add on top of AWS Glue?
cards.back: Fast data lake setup on S3 (blueprints that build Glue workflows) and **centralised fine-grained permissions** (database, table, column, row and cell level, LF-Tags, cross-account sharing) enforced in Athena, Redshift Spectrum, EMR, Glue and Quick Sight.

cards.front: Which sources can Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink read from, and which common one can it NOT?
cards.back: It reads from **Kinesis Data Streams** and **Amazon MSK** (Kafka). It **cannot read from Amazon Data Firehose**; Firehose can only be a destination of a Flink app.

cards.front: Amazon MSK vs Kinesis Data Streams: name three differences.
cards.back: MSK uses **open-source Kafka APIs** (topics and partitions) vs AWS APIs (streams and shards); MSK keeps data **as long as you configure** vs up to 365 days; MSK can only **add** partitions, while Kinesis can split and merge shards. Both use KMS at rest and TLS in transit (MSK also allows plaintext).

cards.front: What is MSK Serverless?
cards.back: A cluster type that runs Apache Kafka **without capacity planning**: MSK provisions and scales compute and storage automatically and bills by throughput. It requires **IAM access control**.

cards.front: In the serverless big data pipeline, what is the role of Firehose, S3 events and Athena?
cards.back: **Firehose** batches the Kinesis stream (optionally transformed by Lambda) into an S3 ingestion bucket in near real time; **S3 event notifications** (via SQS) trigger **Lambda**, which runs an **Athena** query whose results land in a reporting bucket for Quick Sight or Redshift.
